title: Instead of 'Said'
theme: Speech verbs that show how and why a character speaks
objectives: I can use ten speech verbs to show how and why a character speaks.
I can choose a verb that matches a character's feeling and volume.
I can replace said in my writing with a stronger verb.
I can write a short scene where the speech verbs show how characters feel.
rationale: Replacing said is the quickest visible improvement in third-grade narrative writing, and each of these verbs carries a feeling, a volume, or a reason. The ten words sort into loud or sudden voices (exclaim, bellow, blurt, gasp), quiet or unsure voices (murmur, mutter, stammer), and firm voices (declare, protest, plead). The unit builds directly on the character words from unit 1: a boastful character declares, a bashful one murmurs or stammers. Students learn that a verb should be chosen because it fits the moment, not because it is longer than said.

words.def: To take in a quick breath because of surprise or shock.
words.ex: Everyone gasped when the magician pulled a rabbit out of the hat.
words.ex2: She gasped as the icy water splashed over her legs.
words.nonExample: A calm, slow sigh after a long nap is not a gasp.

apps.academic: Authors use gasp to show that a character is shocked.
apps.spoken: I gasped when I saw the huge spider.
apps.writing: Use gasp to show surprise through a breath, not just through words.

cloze.s: The audience began to ___ when the acrobat slipped from the high rope.

cloze2.s: When the lights went out in the dark hallway, Ravi took a sharp breath and had to ___.

misuse.s: He gasped slowly and calmly because nothing surprising had happened all day.
misuse.why: A gasp is a quick breath of surprise; nothing surprising happened here.

visual.alt: A child with wide eyes and an open mouth watching a magic trick.

words.def: To say something suddenly and loudly because of strong feeling.
words.ex2: Dad exclaimed that the sunset was the most beautiful he had ever seen.
words.nonExample: A quiet comment made in a flat voice is not an exclamation.

apps.academic: An exclamation point often follows words that a character exclaims.
apps.writing: Use exclaim for strong feelings such as joy, surprise, or excitement.

cloze.s: "Look at the rainbow!" Tia ___ as she pointed at the sky after the storm.

cloze2.s: When the last goal went in, the whole team ___ with joy and jumped up and down.

misuse.s: "I am so excited," she exclaimed in a flat, bored voice with her eyes half closed.
misuse.why: Exclaim means to speak loudly with strong feeling; a flat, bored voice does not fit.

visual.alt: A child pointing at a rainbow with an exclamation mark above.

words.def: To speak in a low voice that is hard to hear, often when annoyed.
words.ex: The tired boy muttered something about homework and shuffled away.
words.ex2: I could hear Grandpa mutter at the crossword puzzle.
words.nonExample: Cheering loudly for your team is not muttering.

apps.academic: A character who mutters often shows that he or she is unhappy but does not want to say it out loud.
apps.spoken: I muttered, "This is so hard," under my breath.
apps.writing: Use mutter for low, grumpy words that are not meant for everyone to hear.

cloze.s: The cranky driver ___ under his breath when the traffic light turned red again.

cloze2.s: Tina ___ that the game was unfair, but she said it so quietly that no one else heard.

misuse.s: The coach muttered the team's victory speech so loudly that the whole field could hear every word.
misuse.why: Mutter is low and hard to hear; a loud speech is not muttering.

visual.alt: A frowning child speaking with a tiny speech bubble.

words.def: To say something clearly and firmly so everyone hears.
words.ex: The mayor declared that the new park was open.
words.ex2: "I am the fastest runner in the class," she declared.
words.nonExample: Mumbling an unsure guess is not declaring.

apps.academic: A leader may declare a decision so that everyone knows it is final.
apps.spoken: I declare this the best sandwich ever.
apps.writing: Use declare when a character states something with confidence.

cloze.s: The king stood on the steps and ___ that the festival would begin at noon.

cloze2.s: With a proud smile, the girl ___ that she had finished the whole puzzle by herself.

misuse.s: The captain declared the winner in a tiny, unsure voice that no one could hear.
misuse.why: Declare means to say something firmly and clearly; a tiny, unsure voice does not fit.

visual.alt: A king on steps holding up a scroll while people listen.

words.def: To speak very softly in a low, steady voice.
words.ex: The nurse murmured gently to calm the crying baby.
words.ex2: People murmured to each other as the movie began.
words.nonExample: Yelling across a gym is not murmuring.

apps.academic: Soft verbs such as murmur set a calm or secret mood in a story.
apps.spoken: She murmured, "It's okay," to her little brother.
apps.writing: Use murmur for a gentle voice that comforts or tells a secret.

cloze.s: The kind teacher ___ a few calm words to the nervous student before the test began.

cloze2.s: In the quiet library, the readers ___ to each other so they would not disturb anyone.

misuse.s: The singer murmured the last line at the top of her voice so the whole stadium shook.
misuse.why: Murmur means to speak very softly; shouting at the top of your voice is the opposite.

visual.alt: Two children leaning close in a library and speaking softly.

words.def: To say strongly that you disagree or think something is unfair.
words.ex: The students protested when the teacher took away recess.
words.nonExample: Agreeing happily with a plan is not protesting.

apps.academic: In social studies, people protest to show they disagree with a rule.
apps.spoken: I protested when they changed the rules in the middle of the game.
apps.writing: Use protest for a speaker who strongly says no to something unfair.

cloze.s: The campers ___ when the counselor said the lake would be closed all week.

cloze2.s: "I did not take your pencil!" Marcus ___ with a red face.

misuse.s: The class protested the news by cheering and saying they loved the new rule.
misuse.why: Protest means to disagree; cheering for a rule shows agreement.

visual.alt: A child holding up a hand to say stop while looking upset.

words.def: To repeat sounds or pause while speaking, often from nerves.
words.ex: Nervous about the spelling bee, Ana stammered over the first word.
words.ex2: When the principal walked in, the boy stammered and could hardly finish his sentence.
words.nonExample: A speaker who talks smoothly and confidently is not stammering.

apps.academic: A character may stammer when surprised, scared, or embarrassed.
apps.spoken: I stammered because I was nervous about the question.
apps.writing: Use stammer to show nerves or surprise in how a character speaks.

cloze.s: Facing the huge crowd for the first time, the shy singer began to ___ over the first line.

cloze2.s: When the teacher asked a surprise question, Mateo ___ and said, "Um, I, I think so."

misuse.s: She stammered in perfect, smooth sentences and never paused once.
misuse.why: Stammer means repeating sounds or pausing; smooth sentences are the opposite.

visual.alt: A nervous child holding a microphone with a worried face.

words.def: To ask in a serious, begging way for something you really want.
words.ex: The child pleaded with her dad to let her keep the stray kitten.
words.ex2: "Please, please let me stay!" he pleaded.
words.nonExample: Casually saying, "No, thanks," is not pleading.

apps.academic: A character who pleads wants something very much and may feel desperate.
apps.spoken: I pleaded with my mom for ten more minutes.
apps.writing: Use plead to show that a character is begging for help or a chance.

cloze.s: The little boy ___ with the lifeguard to let him jump in one more time.

cloze2.s: With tears in her eyes, Amara ___ for someone to help find her lost dog.

misuse.s: The prince pleaded in a bored voice, and he did not care at all whether anyone helped him.
misuse.why: Plead means to beg because you want something badly; a bored voice does not fit.

visual.alt: A child with hands pressed together asking a parent for a puppy.

words.def: To say something suddenly without thinking first.
words.ex: Ivan blurted out the secret before he could stop himself.
words.ex2: Instead of raising her hand, Tia blurted out the answer.
words.nonExample: Planning each word carefully before you speak is not blurting.

apps.academic: A character who blurts out a secret can cause a problem in a story.
apps.spoken: I blurted out the answer, and then I felt silly.
apps.writing: Use blurt when words come out too fast to stop.

cloze.s: Before anyone could stop him, Noel ___ out the surprise that the class was keeping.

cloze2.s: Excited about the field trip, the girl ___ the news to her mother before taking off her coat.

misuse.s: He blurted out the answer only after thinking about it carefully for ten minutes.
misuse.why: Blurt means to speak suddenly without thinking; ten minutes of thinking is the opposite.

visual.alt: A child covering their mouth after words burst out.

words.def: To shout in a loud, deep voice.
words.ex: The coach bellowed across the field for the team to run faster.
words.ex2: A bull bellowed from the far end of the pasture.
words.nonExample: A soft whisper in a library is not a bellow.

apps.academic: Bellow is a strong verb that shows a very loud, deep voice, such as a bull's or a giant's.
apps.spoken: My uncle bellowed from the other side of the yard.
apps.writing: Use bellow for a very loud, deep voice that carries across a distance.

cloze.s: From the back of the huge gym, the referee ___ so that every player could hear the call.

cloze2.s: The giant in the story ___ with a voice that shook the windows of the whole village.

misuse.s: He bellowed the lullaby in the tiniest whisper so he would not wake the baby.
misuse.why: Bellow means to shout in a loud, deep voice; a tiny whisper is the opposite.

visual.alt: A bull with its mouth open next to a loudspeaker.

passage.title: The Surprise Party
paras: Maya's friends hid behind the couch for her surprise party. Balloons covered the ceiling, and a long banner hung across the wall. When the door opened, they jumped up. Maya gasped. "You did this for me?" she exclaimed.
Her brother Leo bellowed from the kitchen, "The cake is almost ready!" Grandma murmured softly to the baby so he would not cry at the noise.
Then Leo blurted out, "Maya, we got you a puppy!" Everyone groaned. Leo covered his mouth with both hands. Mom had planned to keep that part a secret until after the cake.
Maya stammered, "A-a puppy?" Her voice shook with joy. From a box by the door, a tiny brown dog poked out his nose.

Aunt Rosa protested, "A puppy will chew every shoe in the house!" Grandpa muttered that he did not mind a few chewed shoes. Maya pleaded, "Please, can we keep him?" Dad declared, "He stays." The whole room cheered, and Mom laughed and hugged the little dog.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "blurted" tells us that Leo spoke
qs.why: Leo gave away the secret by accident, so the words came out before he thought.

qs.q: Why did everyone groan after Leo spoke?
qs.why: The puppy was supposed to be a secret, and Leo told it too soon.

qs.q: Which detail shows that Aunt Rosa did not like the idea of a puppy?
choices: She said a puppy would chew every shoe.
She spoke softly to the baby.
qs.why: Aunt Rosa protested with a reason, which shows she disagreed.

choices: She was so surprised and happy that she could not speak smoothly.
qs.why: Her voice shook with joy, which shows her feeling was strong and joyful.

write.prompt: Write a short scene where two characters talk. Do not use said. Use at least three speech verbs from this unit.

study.task: Make a loud-to-quiet line with the ten verbs. Choose one verb and say the same sentence in that voice for a partner. Your partner guesses the verb and tells what feeling it shows.

sentences: Write a sentence about a character who gasped. Tell what surprised the character.
Write a sentence with bellowed. Tell where someone would need a loud voice.
Write a sentence where a character muttered. What was the character unhappy about?
Write a sentence with pleaded. Tell what the character wanted.

combine.model: Leo bellowed from the kitchen that the cake was almost ready.

given: She spoke in a loud, happy voice.
combine.model: Maya gasped, and then she exclaimed that she could not believe it.

discuss: When is a quiet voice such as murmur better than a loud voice?
Is it ever good to blurt? Why or why not?
What is the difference between protest and plead?
produce.explain: Explain why a writer might choose muttered instead of said. Use muttered and a sample sentence.

argue.prompt: Claim: Writers should never use the word said. Do you agree or disagree? Give two reasons.
argue.frame: I agree (or disagree) that ___ because ___. For example, ___.

constructed.prompt: Write two sentences about the same classroom, one with someone who bellows and one with someone who murmurs. Say who spoke and why.
constructed.model: The coach bellowed across the gym so everyone could hear the rules. Later the teacher murmured to a nervous student to help her feel calm.

constructed.prompt: A student wants more time at recess. Write one sentence where the student protests and one where the student pleads.
look: shows disagreement in one and begging in the other
constructed.model: "That is not fair!" Eli protested when recess ended early. "Please, just five more minutes," he pleaded.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten speech verbs that show how and why a character speaks, arrange them by volume and feeling, and use them to replace said in a short dialogue narrative and in their own scenes.

notes.va.gasp.v: Gasp is about the breath, so it often comes before words. Act out a gasp and a calm sigh and ask students which one shows surprise.
notes.va.exclaim.v: Exclaim connects to the exclamation point. Ask students to read a line aloud first quietly, then as if it were exclaimed.
notes.va.mutter.v: Mutter often shows annoyance. It is not the same as whisper, which can be calm. Ask students to read a line as a mutter and as a whisper and compare the mood.
notes.va.declare.v: Declare is firm and public, like making an announcement. Boastful characters from unit 1 often declare things. Practice a declare voice and a murmur voice.
notes.va.murmur.v: Murmur is soft and steady. Compare it with mutter: a murmur can be kind, while a mutter is usually grumpy.
notes.va.protest.v: Protest is verb here (stress on the second syllable). Students may know the noun. Ask what a character protests and why.
notes.va.stammer.v: Teach this word with respect: stammering is also a real speech difference, and students should never use it to tease. In stories it shows nerves; in life it is not a joke.
notes.va.plead.v: Plead is strong asking. Compare ask, beg, and plead on a ladder. Discuss when pleading is a good choice and when a calm request is better.
notes.va.blurt.v: Blurt is speech that gets ahead of thinking. Link to the unit 1 word bashful: bashful characters rarely blurt. Ask what a character could do instead of blurting.
notes.va.bellow.v: Bellow is both loud and deep. Have students try a high shout and a bellow and tell the difference. Link to gigantic: giants bellow.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The text says Leo bellowed from the kitchen. He is far away, so he needs a loud, deep voice. If the author wrote said, I would not hear how loud he was. Bellowed tells me volume and distance. I choose a verb that gives the reader the voice.'
discuss: Which speech verb would a bashful character use? Which would a boastful character use?
When might said be the best word to use?
misconceptions: Said is a bad word and should never be used.
A longer verb is always better than said.
Stammer means being rude or silly.
Murmur and mutter mean exactly the same thing.
extend: Rewrite a dialogue from a book by replacing each said with a more exact verb and read it aloud.
Draw a comic strip with speech bubbles and label each bubble with one verb from the unit.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the loud-to-quiet line two days later with a new sentence, and again after a week. Link boastful, bashful, and gigantic from earlier units by asking which verb each character would use.

frames: I think ___ would murmur when ___, but would bellow when ___.
wida.oral: Partner A reads a short sentence in the voice of one verb from the unit without naming it. Partner B guesses the verb and says what feeling the voice showed.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (soltar un grito ahogado, refunfuñar, tartamudear, suplicar, soltar, bramar) are not reviewed by a native speaker; gasp and blurt have no single Spanish verb.
Stammer is taught with a note about respect for people who have a speech difference; the teacher should adapt the discussion to the class.
Check the volume ladder order (mutter versus declare) for third graders; it is a teaching ladder, not a dictionary ranking.
